div.head: COMMON THREATS TO RI SGCN AND SOME SOLUTIONS
div.p: It is best to consider threats and actions as they relate to one another, and these links are presented in the RIWAP database. The threats summarized below are intended only as a high-level summary of some of the most prevalent threats from the database coupled with some key conservation needs.

div.head: HABITAT LOSS, FRAGMENTATION, AND DEGRADATION OF KEY HABITAT
div.p: A primary threat to Rhode Island's fish, wildlife, and their habitats is loss of natural areas to human development (e.g., buildings, parking lots, roads, energy, and recreational uses Fragmentation subdivides large contiguous areas of natural land into smaller patches, resulting in each patch having more edge habitat and less interior. This can be a problem for many species, particularly species that rely on large patches of the same plant community or vegetative structure (e.g., interior forest for Marbled Salamander, Wood Thrush, and Scarlet Tanager). Thus, fragmentation can lead to an overall deterioration of ecological quality and integrity, and a shift in associated species from interior specialists to edge generalists.

Because the future of Rhode Island's wildlife will rely on the amount of habitat remaining, fee acquisition and easements that protect land will continue to be among the most important components of this SWAP. Acquisition, in conjunction with effective preserve design and focal area approaches (see below), has the greatest potential to protect the most species for the longest time.

No other suite of strategies can mitigate for a lack of habitat, so land protection strategies are key. To effectively conserve all SGCN, some wildlife preserves will need to be continually managed to reduce detrimental impacts associated with poor habitat quality, increased predation, nest parasitism by Brown-headed Cowbirds, contamination from outside sources, invasive species, human disturbance, and a changing climate.
Advanced spatial planning and prioritization is a critical first step.

div.head: INVASIVE AND OTHER PROBLEMATIC SPECIES
div.p: The spread of invasive species poses a significant threat to SGCN throughout the Northeast. Invasive species go by many names, but all are introduced, non-indigenous organisms that can aggressively displace and overtake populations of native species and devastate natural habitats. These invasives are most often plants, and most SGCN are indirectly impacted by their spread. The changes most evident in an invaded community are declines in native plant diversity and a consequent restructuring of the community that very often negatively alters habitats of SGCN. Animals, such as non-native crabs in marsh systems, invasive invertebrates like Asian shore crabs and fouling tunicates like Didemnum in marine environments, outdoor cats that kill 1.3-4 billion birds and 6. The Rhode Island Invasive Species Council (RIISC) maintains a list of plants considered invasive, and both freshwater aquatic and marine invasives have been tracked for decades. Still, resources do not match the scale of the problem, and Rhode Island does not have comprehensive legislation to prevent even intentional introductions of invasive species not otherwise subject to prohibitions. Prevention is far more cost-effective than control once a species has taken hold in an area.

While invasives are, by definition, non-native species, "problematic" species can include opportunistic native species that can disrupt more sensitive native species when ecological systems get out of balance. Examples include Brown-headed Cowbird, a nest parasite; carnivores raiding bird and turtle nests; and deer over browsing native plant communities. Human disturbance is closely linked to this threat, whether it is from newly colonizing species or native species out of balance. Brown-headed Cowbirds are very successful in fragmented forests; carnivores like skunks and raccoons thrive alongside humans, where they are subsidized when we leave pet food outside or trash unsecured; and the elimination of larger predators and fragmentation of habitats by humans has contributed to the high density of deer in Southern New England.

Like the negative impacts of development, the best way to address the impacts of invasive and problematic species is to first plan to avoid as many as possible. For example, RIDEM has implemented protocols since the 2015 Plan to minimize the spread of problematic plants, animals, and pathogens during survey work that mandate cleaning and sterilization of gear between visits to different vernal pools. And Northeast states have increased their coordination and information sharing to maximize efficiency preventing and addressing disease outbreaks. The RIISC, which had not been active since 2005, reconvened and updated its list of invasive and weedy plants in Rhode Island in 2020, and several RIDEM, partners, and other volunteer programs and partnerships monitor terrestrial, aquatic, and marine invasive species in different habitats or throughout Rhode Island. Still, a terrestrial equivalent to the state's Aquatic Species Management Plan has yet to be completed, and full prevention would include an institutionalized framework and increased efforts to promote the appreciation, restoration, and stewardship of our native ecology.

div.head: CLIMATE CHANGE AND SEVERE WEATHER
div.p: As described in Chapter 2, Rhode Island is already experiencing the impacts of climate change, and these are expected to interact with and compound the effects of most other threats (e.g., milder winters allow more introduced species to establish, extreme summer temperatures and drought will further shrink access to cool water refugia on dammed streams). Average and extreme temperatures and precipitation are all projected to increase in the Northeast, although the magnitude of increases will depend on human behavior and the resultant trajectory of

div.head: THREATS AND ACTIONS
div.p: greenhouse gas emissions. Climate models identify 2035-2040 as the critical point when future scenario projections begin to diverge dramatically depending on emissions. In a medium emissions scenario, by 2100 RI is projected to experience as much as an additional up to 7˚F warming a tenfold increase in days with temperatures above 95˚F , up to 45% increase in precipitation, roughly 40% increase in the number of days per year with precipitation above 1 inch relative to the current climate, and more days per year with extreme precipitation across the state. Increasing temperatures will mean more rain and less snow (Staudinger et al. 2025).

One There are many places where both the NECASC climate synthesis and the RIWAP database call out the need for additional information. At the same time, action is needed now, and we know enough to begin to act. Without state capacity or even expertise for many of the taxa addressed in the RIWAP, one of the primary responsibilities of the State is to work to conserve the integrity and connectedness of "the stage" upon which all these species' live. This is supported by Staudinger et al. 2024 in, for example, the actions menu provided with focal topics and example approaches to address climate stressors. Many RIWAP database actions match the spirit of these projects (e.g., protect and steward remaining intact core forest habitats, identify and protect cold water habitat, reconnect high quality stream reaches and re-establish in-stream flows, retain and increase shade along banks, and increase coordination to steward native plants and native seed networks).

div.head: NATURAL SYSTEM MODIFICATIONS
div.p: Natural system modifications are defined as conversions or degradations of habitat in service of "managing" natural or seminatural systems, often to improve human welfare (Salafsky et al. 2008). The damming of rivers and streams is an example of a direct habitat modification, but some modifications involve the suppression of natural disturbances that, if allowed to occur under normal frequencies and intensities, could result in damage to property and/or loss of life, such as fire or flooding. This suppression or management of natural disturbance often results in the minimization or elimination of processes essential to the maintenance of natural communities.

div.head: THREATS AND ACTIONS
div.p: While lightning-strike fires are relatively rare events in southern New England compared to much of the country, Rhode Island nevertheless has fire-dependent habitats, particularly pitch pine. Although there is little historical evidence that fire was purposely used to generate sizable areas of open habitat (Foster and Motzkin 2002), Indigenous peoples employed fire as a land management tool across the region, and it is apparent that such selective burning helped create and maintain firedependent habitats in southern New England, especially Pitch Pine barrens. Lack of fire in Pitch Pine barrens results in succession of these communities with an increase in hardwoods and reduction in Scrub Oak understories that support the unique assemblage of plants and animals characteristic of barrens habitats, many of which depend on fire to reduce competition from fire-intolerant species or to stimulate a physiological response, such as the high temperatures needed to release the seeds from Pitch Pine cones. Recognition of this consequence of fire suppression has spurred conservation organizations and agencies throughout the Northeast to conduct controlled burns to manage Pitch Pine barrens and other fire dependent habitats, and RIDEM continues to work to expand its capacity and outreach to conduct controlled burns as appropriate.

Another common threat to many aquatic species and wetland habitats is water management, including dam construction, surface water diversion, withdrawals from surface and groundwater sources, and other operations that alter water flow patterns from their natural range of variation either deliberately or as a result of other activities. Rhode Island has a long history of water management, particularly for mills and reservoirs. Of particular concern to fish and wildlife resources is the construction of dams on major rivers that has prevented the migration of anadromous fish to inland breeding locations and impeded the inland flow of tidal waters, resulting in the nearly total loss of Freshwater Tidal Marshes.

div.head: POLLUTION
div.p: The Northeast consists of some of the highest population densities and oldest buildings and infrastructure. The combination of large metropolitan areas, thriving industries, often out-of-date septic and wastewater systems, and legacy contaminants generates significant amounts of waste in the form of household sewage, solid waste, industrial effluents, and leachate. Pollutants from these sources impair key riparian, aquatic, and terrestrial habitats throughout the region. Changes in water quality and quantity pose serious threats to all northeastern aquatic systems. As urbanization increases and natural vegetated buffers decline, natural filters for toxins are lost and they make their way directly into surface waters in runoff and sediments. The evidence for negative impacts from noise and light pollution are accumulating as well, and the use of outdoor lighting has grown exponentially (Kyba et al. 2017). As natural areas and canopy cover decline, the impacts of noise and light pollution also travel further across the landscape.

One recurrent pollution threat in the RIWAP is pesticides. By their nature, substances that are designed to kill pests can pose risks to humans and the environment. The organic farming community in the state remains a bright spot and factor in more recent curtailments of pesticides (including herbicides) and fertilizers, but improvements are still needed. Additionally, excessive use of fertilizers and pesticides by homeowners and other land managers is still a nearly ubiquitous threat across the state and actions to raise awareness, restrict by law or policy, and incentivize behavior change are found in the RIWAP database.
In the marine environment, drifting debris and microplastics also pose serious threats to wildlife.
Drifting marine debris can result in entanglements of marine mammals, fish, and sea turtles.
Microplastics have been found extensively in Narragansett Bay, outflowing rivers and marine sediments and have been shown to accumulate in the tissues of some species.

div.head: BIOLOGICAL RESOURCE USE
div.p: This category includes deliberate and unintentional harvesting, as well as the persecution or control of specific species (Salafsky et al. 2008). Several SGCN birds and mammals are game species and therefore subject to "deliberate harvesting," and related actions include commitments to iteratively assess the impacts of harvest and, with it, limits and seasons as applicable. A variety of marine fish and invertebrates are also subject to deliberate harvesting through both commercial and recreational

div.head: THREATS AND ACTIONS
div.p: means. Their harvest is managed through science-based decision-making. The take of species from the wild has also been identified as an issue for 52% of SGCN reptiles and amphibians, primarily due to illegal collecting of these animals for the pet trade. Interdisciplinary efforts have increased throughout the Northeast to curb wildlife trafficking, from universities providing education to students, to increased knowledge of and attention to the issue from law enforcement, to recovered species stewardship and repatriation with the support of zoos and other partners.

div.head: HUMAN DISTURBANCE
div.p: This category includes threats from human activities that alter, destroy and disturb habitats and species associated with non-consumptive uses of biological resources (Salafsky et al. 2008). In a state with a high population density, the threat of human disturbance to many fish and wildlife species and their habitats can be considerable, and those species most sensitive to human presence are among the most vulnerable and most challenging to protect. In Rhode Island, most existing preserves are not large enough to support vulnerable species, due to pressures from public use and indirect influences from surrounding land uses. Therefore, a strategy of increasing the size of protected preserves is appropriate. RIDEM has typically prioritized new acquisition projects by their adjacency to existing open space, or that are inholdings within protected lands. Historically, this has been done largely to preserve or expand traditional recreational activities, but the spatial requirements of some of Rhode Island's SGCN has increased the urgency of preserving large parcels of contiguous habitat.

If acquisitions are prioritized with wildlife conservation as a primary goal, then issues such as habitat management, additive mortality of animals, and connectivity can be more strategically addressed.
Where public access is provided, it can be routed to skirt relatively remote habitat cores.

There are numerous examples of this threat that extend beyond insufficient preserve size. For example, maritime beaches and the unique suite of species they support are vulnerable because of the extreme use of these habitats for human recreation. Beach-nesting birds, including piping plover and least tern, are particularly vulnerable because human disturbance often curtails breeding success.

Foot and vehicular traffic may crush nests or young and excessive disturbance may cause the parents to desert the nest, exposing eggs or chicks to the summer sun and predators. Pets, especially dogs, may harass the birds, and developments near beaches provide food that attracts increased numbers of predators such as raccoons, skunks, and foxes. Additionally, compaction from driving on beaches was thought to be the primary cause for the loss of the northeastern beach tiger beetle from Rhode Island and that led to its listing as a federally threatened species. Interior sand flats and barrens also support rare tiger beetles, and even protected sites may be overrun and degraded by illegal off-road vehicle use. More aggressive protection of such habitat types is clearly indicated. The broader issue of human intrusions and disturbance across habitats will require education and outreach to increase awareness and creative solutions that balance minimal disturbance to critical habitats with thoughtful enjoyment of natural lands.

div.head: NEW ENERGY DEVELOPMENTS
div.p: The Block Island Wind Farm, the nation's first offshore wind farm, was installed since the 2015 RIWAP was published. Terrestrial wind projects have slowed as municipalities have begun to enact guardrails on this type of development. The rapid expansion of industrial scale solar panel installations is a more recent concern, primarily because of the land they consume. Wind turbines can pose a threat to birds, although they appear to be a relatively minor source of concern compared to other sources of fatality at the current rate of development (e.g., collisions with buildings and communication towers and predation by cats). The degree of threat to bats is still not fully understood, but there have been developments in avoidance technology (curtailment), which are recommended to be included in permitting in the RIWAP as well as an in-process Guidelines for Wildlife Management and Renewable Energy in the Northeast commissioned as part of a larger RCN project (Canino and Grodsky, in progress). Offshore wind poses both threats and potential benefits to a variety of marine species. Construction presents with the possibility of pile-driving noise, habitat disturbance or destruction, and increased vessel activity in the area, while operation creates different anthropogenic changes such as operational noise, generation of electromagnetic fields, and added hardbottom habitat. This is an area of active research, as effects of offshore wind development on species in the Northwest Atlantic are not well understood at this time.

div.head: LACK OF INFORMATION, PLANNING, AND CAPACITY
div.p: Although not direct threats, lack of information, planning, and capacity, including capacity for muchneeded outreach and coordination, are some of the most important stumbling blocks to conservation. Accurate information on the distribution, status, and ecology of SGCN and key habitats is critical to respond appropriately and meaningfully to identified threats. Bright spots include the publication of books on the reptiles, amphibians, Odonates, and birds of Rhode Island, the development of community science apps (e.g., Herp Observer, Bee Observer, Songbird Mortality Report), and participatory science with trained volunteers (e.g., RI Bird Atlas 2.0 and the Rhode Island Bumble Bee and Wild Bee Surveys), all of which have increased access to distribution data. However, primarily due to budgetary constraints, there has been little accomplished regarding the acquisition and management of data to complete conservation actions identified in the RIWAP. The same is true with the need for outreach and dissemination of information and capacity to carry out needed conservation and management actions. This problem is greatly exacerbated for the more than half of SGCN that are not traditionally hunted or fished, as the only consistent and meaningful funding for all but mammals, birds, and finfish across RIDEM is SWG. This funding has remained relatively static, while the species in need and cost of doing this work have increased substantially.

The number of priority needs and actions identified during this process will require significant effort within RIDEM. However, the extent to which it can be implemented is also dependent upon external factors outside of RIDEM's control. Specific actions that will better enable RIDEM to implement this RIWAP include increasing advocacy for conservation, increasing agency resources and capacity for conservation, and establishing dedicated state funding for work on SGCN and their key habitats.

One major way that Northeast states mitigate capacity gaps is through regional coordination. The close proximity of many northeastern states has engendered a long history of cooperative and/ or complementary management approaches, including a strong technical committee structure.

Technical committees are species or habitat-focused groups that exchange ideas and develop common approaches to wildlife issues, as described more in Chapter 1. Typically, these actions are implemented by individual states using their own funds; however, in some cases additional funding has been made available through the Northeast Directors.

The RCN Program formalizes a cooperative approach to address SGCN needs across multiple states and aims to develop, coordinate, and implement conservation actions that are regional/sub-regional in scope and build upon the many regional initiatives that already exist. The RCN program utilizes a funding mechanism that is equitable to all Northeast states and Washington, D.C, creating a base of funding for regional projects. Since 2007, fifty-three different projects have been completed. The resulting reports and products can be found at https://northeastwildlifediversity.org. The resources identified on this map are intended to capture habitats with high conservation value by identifying the largest intact and connected blocks of common habitats, as well as other unique places based on rare, resilient, or productive natural systems. This map is a general guide for strategic investment in Rhode Island's natural areas.

div.head: CONSERVATION OPPORTUNITY AREAS: AN OVERARCHING APPROACH TO CONSERVATION PLANNING
THREATS AND ACTIONS
div.p: COAs should be considered priority areas for conserving Rhode Island's SGCN and key habitats.

COAs contain and highlight locations with significant existing or potential wildlife and habitat resources and areas where partners can contribute to plan, implement, and evaluate conservation actions Still, it must be understood that not all listed species occur within this set of locations, and restricting conservation actions to these areas will not necessarily maintain viable populations or meet the objectives outlined in the RIWAP. It should also be noted that many restoration opportunities exist outside these COAs that can contribute significantly to conservation in RI, especially in developed areas.

This COA map is intended for general planning purposes only. It should not be used for legal boundary definition, regulatory interpretation, or property conveyance purposes. The resources identified on this map are intended to capture habitats with high conservation value by identifying the largest intact and connected blocks of common habitats, as well as other unique places based on rare, resilient, or productive natural systems. This map provides a general guide for strategic investment in Rhode Island's natural areas and is not intended as a comprehensive inventory of all valuable natural habitats. This facilitates incorporation of the COAs into the Statewide Planning process and local land use Comprehensive Plans. Next steps should include developing customized municipal information, maps and plans at a finer scale through a cooperative local planning process to incorporate these SWAP priorities into local land use decisions.
The following features were mapped to create the RIWAP COAs (available in the RIDEM Map Room):

• Unfragmented Forested Blocks: The heart of the map is the unfragmented forest blocks of 500 acres or greater. These blocks constitute the 'core natural areas' and capture the best (largest and least fragmented) examples of common forest habitats as well as many rarer imbedded natural systems. Unfragmented forest blocks of between 250 and 500 acres may be important as connectors between the larger blocks.

• Habitats with high habitat value and high vulnerability: SWAP Key Habitats ranked highest for Biodiversity Value and Vulnerability (Floodplain, Hemlock/Hardwood, and Northern Hardwood Forests; Pitch Pine Woodland/ Barrens and Inland Sand Barrens; Wet Meadow, Sea Level Fens, and Atlantic White Cedar Swamp; Coastal Streams and Freshwater Tidal Marsh; Mud Flats, Sand Flats, Salt Marsh, and Brackish Marsh; Rocky Shore; and Brackish Sub-aquatic Beds).

• Other diverse or otherwise important habitats: These include Rhode Island's Natural Heritage Areas as well as places with a high Ecological Land Unit (ELU) diversity. Places categorized as 'better' or 'best' in terms of ELU diversity capture areas with a diverse assemblage of landform, soil drainage class, and soil texture. This diverse structure will remain relatively unchanged by shifting climate and provides an opportunity for diverse assemblages of plant communities and fauna to persist. The sites with diverse ELU types will likely host a variety of microclimates that provide opportunities for natural communities to shift and persevere in the face of changing temperature and precipitation patterns.

• Important Coastal Habitats: These important natural places along Rhode Island's shore include important bird stopover sites made up of coastal shrubland systems on the north end of Block Island and the western shore of Little Compton; conservation targets identified by TNC's North Atlantic Coast Ecoregional Assessment, including the best regional examples of salt marsh, rocky shore, beaches, dunes, and coastal lagoons (salt ponds); and coastal wetlands identified as IBAs .

• Marine and Estuarine Systems: All state waters (defined as up to 3 nautical miles from shore) in Rhode Island and Block Island Sounds have been identified as important marine and estuarine systems, both incredibly productive and globally significant.
• Major and Minor Corridors: Corridors connect natural core areas and smaller habitats on the landscape and allow for the movement of both migrating species and species within their ranges.
They also allow for the movement of habitat types, populations, and gene flow among populations and locations as species shift in response to climate change. Major and minor corridors are

div.head: THREATS AND ACTIONS
div.p: identified based on the locations of the core natural areas and other important natural systems identified above in relation to one another. These were informed by TNC's regional connectivity analysis, part of the Northeast Terrestrial Resilience project, as well as by the location of natural corridors provided by existing river systems.

• Freshwater Connectivity Opportunities: The many obsolete dams found on Rhode Island's river systems create barriers to fish migration and provide opportunities to enhance river connectivity with their removal. TNC and RIDEM have identified these freshwater connectivity opportunities by mapping the first impediment (dam) on each reach of river encountered when traveling upstream from the ocean. Connected waterways can be expanded toward the headwaters as these barriers are removed.

Conservation opportunities are not only land conservation projects; they also include land management strategies and a variety of natural system restoration opportunities. In freshwater river systems, maximum habitat availability and function are provided when fish can move unimpeded between headwater streams, estuaries, and marine environments. Conserving COAs will require the efforts of many conservation partners working together to incorporate it into their programs and plans.

div.head: NEXT STEPS-FOCAL AREAS
div.p: The COA process should be considered preliminary and dynamic with additional work needed to improve and advance this mapping. A key action from 2015 that remains to be undertaken is to develop focal area and spatially specific focal species approaches in Rhode Island to inform a more data driven COA map.

The focal area approach is a form of biological triage. Focal areas should be large and shaped roughly like circles or squares (to maximize roadless core areas). This approach does not claim that small preserves near urban centers are without biological value -certainly some species will persist in those places. However, if the RIWAP is to protect viable populations of all species at the state scale, then the more difficult challenges will lie with species that require large tracts of contiguous habitat. Some species will not be preserved because we have already lost the opportunity to provide large enough areas. There are no clear answers to how much area and how many individuals are needed to ensure the long-term persistence of any given population and this varies dramatically by species.

Measuring population viability for a species requires the spatial requirements and population structure but population models are unavailable for most species and historical data, even to the presenceabsence level, can be unreliable. However, because vegetation communities and their spatial attributes can help predict areas that may contain viable fish and wildlife populations, those metrics can be used to identify focal areas.

First, focal areas must be large. When considering forest habitats for example, research has shown that many forest interior birds require several thousand acres of unfragmented habitat, and planning for focal areas of this size in Rhode Island is a difficult process. Second, the approach should be stratified according to the various land masses of Rhode Island. For example, all large islands should be treated independently -a focal approach on Block Island would occur at a different spatial scale than one for western Rhode Island. Lastly, focal areas should have roadless cores as large as possible and should ideally, but not necessarily, have a significant proportion of protected acreage. A model focal area will have a core of protected land surrounded by a buffer zone of varying extent where the goal will be to maximize the integrity of the overall preserve. The present COA map is a step in the right direction and contains many elements that would inform a more precise tailoring of Rhode Island's spatial priorities by marrying the landscape geometry and habitat information of the current version of the map with more detailed spatial data for focal species.

CHAPTER 4
Monitoring and Adaptive Management

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Monitoring Rhode Island's SGCN, their habitats, and conservation outcomes is necessary for RIDEM and its partners to determine the effectiveness of conservation actions to address threats facing the state's fish and wildlife. As conditions change (e.g., land use patterns, climate change, global or national population trends, new data), adaptive management and implementation of RIWAP conservation actions identified in the RIWAP database will enable RIDEM to respond appropriately and make efficient use of limited staffing and funds. Rhode Island's approach identifies monitoring efforts and tools currently used by RIDEM or its partners to assess SGCN, key habitats and related issues, as listed in the accompanying RIWAP database.

If monitoring is not identified for an SGCN or species group/taxa, the database describes monitoring actions for other species that occupy the same habitats and/or for their habitats; these recommendations are prioritized to benefit the overall habitat, community, or assemblage, including many other SGCN. In cases where not enough information exists to monitor a species or group, or for which monitoring protocols have not yet been developed, this need is documented and followed by a conservation action intended to address that information need. This is true for some taxa, including many invertebrate groups for which standardized protocols need to be developed and baseline data do not exist to form the basis of a monitoring protocol. As information gaps are filled, any relevant monitoring can be adapted to be more quantitative and specific.

This chapter describes how Rhode Island will use tools for information management and conservation planning to track the implementation and effectiveness of conservation actions through an adaptive management framework. These tools, which are inclusive of and build upon previous frameworks such as the Northeast Regional Monitoring and Performance Reporting Framework (NEAFWA 2008) and Measuring the Effectiveness of State Wildlife Grants (AFWA 2011), are the Northeast Lexicon Project (Crisfield and NEFWDTC 2022), and the USFWS's national Wildlife Tracking and Reporting Actions for the Conservation of Species (Wildlife TRACS). Key species and habitat monitoring Conservation actions will be monitored and measured throughout the 10-year implementation of the RIWAP.

div.head: REGIONAL COORDINATION AND CONTEXT
div.p: NEFWDTC planning efforts have led to several key monitoring projects funded by the RCN Grant Program, and the development and support of regional monitoring activities and partnerships remain a high priority of the NEFWDTC and in the RIWAP. Several key factors cited by the NEFWDTC in supporting the development of regional monitoring activities include the large number of shared priority species and habitats, the relatively limited funding available in any one state for monitoring and evaluation activities, and the presence of many regional experts with knowledge of particular taxa or ecosystems throughout the Northeast.

div.head: CONSERVATION STATUS OF NORTHEAST FISH, WILDLIFE, AND NATURAL HABITATS
div.p: Using indicators developed at the regional level, NEAFWA supported TNC to assess the current condition of species and habitats in the Northeast through the Conservation Status Project. This project used a GIS analysis to examine the relationship between species and habitat condition and land ownership and conservation management status. The original assessment project merged with

div.head: WILDLIFE TRACS DATABASE
div.p: Building on the Northeastern Regional Monitoring and Performance Measures Framework (NEAFWA 2008), the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies (AFWA) led an effort to develop effectiveness measures for wildlife conservation activities funded under the USFWS's SWG program (AFWA 2011).

The effectiveness measures report then informed the development of Wildlife TRACS, a database designed by the USFWS to record information about conservation activities funded through the Office of Conservation Investment (formerly the Wildlife and Sport Fish Restoration Program), including SWG. Wildlife TRACS is intended to track and report project outputs, effectiveness measures, and species and habitat outcomes. It further has the potential to track long-term outcomes for species and habitats, above and beyond the short-term output measures (e.g., number of publications, number of workshops, number of people contacted) commonly tracked by funding agencies. Because it is being designed to be responsive to the needs of the state agencies receiving SWG funding, Wildlife TRACS includes its own customized classifications of conservation actions and threats. These

div.head: NORTHEAST LEXICON FOR COMMON PLANNING AND STATE WILDLIFE ACTION PLAN DATABASE
div.p: Wildlife conservation planners in the Northeast have long recognized the need for a standard lexicon with uniform terminology to accurately describe the work of state fish and wildlife agencies and facilitate identification of regional needs and priorities from Northeast SWAPs. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and CMP have developed lexicons designed primarily for international conservation and sustainable development projects, but such activities differ in important ways from fish and wildlife conservation activities in the Northeast. Thus, the NEFWDTC developed a regional conservation lexicon in 2013, which was updated for the 2025 SWAP revisions (Crisfield and NEFWDTC 2022). The Northeast SWAP Database, originally developed by Terwilliger Consulting, Inc. for the NEFWDTC, was updated by DJ Case and Associates for the 2025 SWAPs and to ensure consistency with the 2022 Northeast Lexicon. This database provides a structure for storing, querying, and comparing across data collected by the individual states and will hold data for all Northeast States once all SWAPs are complete (https://northeastwildlifediversity.org/).

div.head: REGION-WIDE, TAXA-SPECIFIC SURVEY AND MONITORING
div.p: Numerous taxa-specific surveys, inventory, or monitoring programs have been developed and implemented with NEAFWA's support and through other regional collaborations. With RCN funding, surveys and assessments have been conducted for Wood, Box, and Spotted Turtle, pollinators, and many more. More in-depth reports describing the methods and results of these surveys and associated data products are available on the NEFWDTC website.

div.head: MONITORING AND ADAPTIVE MANAGEMENT OF RHODE ISLAND'S SPECIES AND HABITATS
div.p: Rhode Island is committed to an adaptive management approach to fish and wildlife conservation and will track effectiveness measures to obtain the information necessary to do so (Figure 4-1).

Rhode Island has numerous programs that monitor individual wildlife species or species guilds MONITORING/ADAPTIVE MANAGEMENT (e.g., shorebirds, waterfowl), as well as various attributes of wildlife habitats, from the local level to statewide and regional levels. These will remain the primary method for monitoring and tracking SGCN and the condition, extent, and status of wildlife habitats identified in this RIWAP.

Data from these programs and processrelated information from individual implementation projects (e.g. number of meetings held, number of reports produced, number of people contacted through outreach efforts, number of plans developed) will be reported to the USFWS and tracked using the Wildlife TRACS database and shared with the relevant wildlife managers at the state and federal level to inform adaptive management.

The RIWAP database shows ongoing and recently completed wildlife species and habitat survey and monitoring programs that informed the 2025 RIWAP revision and was developed for the first edition of the RIWAP and is updated iteratively. The database lists individual monitoring programs, the associated organization(s) with each program, and the type and level of monitoring, whether single-species, guild-focused, or habitat-focused. Monitoring efforts listed in the RIWAP database have been designed for different purposes and may track different attributes of individual species, groups of species, or of individual sites or ecological communities depending on the management needs of the species or area in question, the level of data needed by wildlife managers, and available resources. Thus, the existing monitoring programs in Rhode Island may not all be reporting similar types of data for all species or habitats that are being tracked in the state. The list is not exhaustive; deer, for example, are omitted because they are abundant.

div.head: IMPORTANT DATA GAPS IN RHODE ISLAND
div.p: With limited resources available to support monitoring programs, it is simply not possible to monitor many aspects of the natural or human environment relevant to fish and wildlife conservation efforts.

Still, it is possible to identify high-priority target areas where additional data would be helpful for developing management prescriptions for fish and wildlife species and their habitats in Rhode Island.

The RIWAP addresses data gaps extensively through identified threats and actions, and some high priority data gaps identified by taxa experts, planners, and stakeholders through iterative RIWAP review, as well as progress toward filling them, are described below. RIDEM and partners continue to work together to develop monitoring programs to address these gaps including species, taxa, habitat and community-level monitoring. This will be an important step towards providing wildlife managers in Rhode Island with the information they need. As of April 2026, the atlas of Rhode Island's bees will be complete. Unfortunately, the RI Pollinator Atlas grant will also close and DFW will no longer have a Pollinator Entomologist position or expertise in invertebrates and insects. This, in addition to loss of staff at other partner organizations in Rhode Island, leaves a large gap in expertise and capacity for future work at the state level. Also, as noted in Chapter 1, data collection even for the state's rarest species has been under resourced for decades and much of the Natural Heritage data is out-of-date.

Broadly, RIDEM's Division of Marine Fisheries (DMF) hopes to utilize SWG funding to address research needs and to better reach its ecosystem-based management goals. The population status and dynamics of most marine species are not well understood, and additional resources are required to reach research and conservation objectives, particularly in the face of a changing climate. Some key priorities include expanding the acoustic telemetry monitoring program to track the movement and seasonality of SGCN species; conducting population assessments; developing habitat suitability models; restoring and enhancing shellfish beds, submerged aquatic vegetation, and other key marine habitats; and gaining a better understanding of the population levels of invasive species and their effects on native species.

div.head: COORDINATION WITH PARTNERS
div.p: Rhode Island has a rich history of collaborative efforts, and existing monitoring efforts captured in the RIWAP database include those of key partners. Likewise, shared survey and tools are used by RIDEM and its partners to assess and adaptively manage SGCN and key habitats and to iteratively update the RIWAP to identify information and research needs, prioritized for species, taxa or habitat.

Creating new programs to address these needs will require extensive coordination. RIDEM will play a lead role, involving key partners and stakeholders in identifying new or expanding current monitoring programs that can be implemented by federal, state and local governments, non-governmental organizations, universities and other partners.

Rhode Island has a unique opportunity though the Rhode Island Environmental Monitoring Collaborative (RIEMC) to coordinate with partners on monitoring programs in the state. The RIEMC provides significant direction and guidance for overall environmental monitoring. Regular annual coordination of all the key partners assures that the opportunity to implement the RIWAP will continue through the RIEMC, as established by the state for this purpose.

div.head: EFFECTIVENESS OF CONSERVATION ACTIONS
div.p: The purpose of tracking effectiveness measures is to obtain the information needed to adaptively manage fish and wildlife species and habitats in the state. The effectiveness of RIWAP conservation actions will be measured using a set of standardized effectiveness measures that have been developed by AFWA and described in their 2011 Measuring the Effectiveness of State Wildlife Grants Final Report (AFWA 2011). In accordance with current limited capacity, effectiveness measures will be tracked for particular classes of conservation actions and reported and tracked as part of RIDEM's regular reporting to the USFWS via the Wildlife TRACS database. Comparisons of the values of these tracked measures over time will begin to indicate the degree of effectiveness of individual projects as well as broader conservation programs.

Implementation performance indicators measure overall plan success based on guiding principles for conservation actions . Once an action is undertaken, information on all indicators may be collected initially; however, it is anticipated that, with experience, a subset will be selected that best measures the effectiveness of the RIWAP as a whole. The evaluation of conservation actions will continue annually through project reporting in TRACS and Federal Aid reports, and as new information becomes available. Annual federal assistance reports will provide new information from SWG and other Federal Aid projects that will be entered into TRACS, the RIWAP database, and GIS spatial coverages to capture successes, changes in SGCN and key habitat status, and the effectiveness of actions. RIDEM staff and technical committees will assess the status of SGCN and key habitats as new data are entered annually or at the end of these projects.

CHAPTER 5 10-Year Review Procedure

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: The RIWAP recognizes the changing state of knowledge and is intended as a dynamic document.

As data gaps are filled, including via recent and ongoing monitoring discussed in Chapter 4, new ones will be identified. The resulting increases in scientific knowledge on which this RIWAP is based will keep the strategy as up to date as possible. This enables better, more informed management decisions that make the best use of limited conservation funding and staffing resources.

RIDEM's and partners' intersecting operational, conservation, and management plans and scheduled program updates provide natural inflection points for periodic review of RIWAP content and implementation. Just as these plans inform RIWAP review and revision, relevant plans are targeted for the inclusion of RIWAP information and conservation actions into their revisions.

The RIWAP is a broad and flexible plan intended to include all the conservation actions needed to secure Rhode Island's full complement of natural communities and the life they support. It also makes clear that far more resources are needed than are presently on hand to accomplish all this work. As such, the adaptive management and other adjustments to implementation described above may or may not require interim changes to the RIWAP itself prior to the 2035 10-year update.

div.head: RIWAP REVIEW SCHEDULE
div.p: While the evaluation of conservation actions will continue annually through Annual Project Reporting in TRACS and Federal Aid reports and as new information becomes available, the RIWAP document will be amended as needed and revised every ten years. A five-year review and evaluation schedule is the most common timeframe for existing management plans in Rhode Island, and Federal Assistance (Application for Federal Assistance-AFA) reporting is also consistent with those plans. This 10-year revision will build upon improvements to the RIWAP to date and incorporate all relevant annual, biannual, and 5-year review and evaluation information and updates so the 10-year revision will not be a total rewriting, but instead an incremental and iterative review and revision process. Annual federal assistance reports will provide new information from SWG and other Federal Aid projects which will be entered into TRACS, the RIWAP database, and RI GIS/RIDEM GIS spatial data to capture and update the annual accomplishments, changes in SGCN and key habitat status, and the effectiveness of actions. RIDEM staff and technical committees will assess the status of SGCN and key habitats as new data are available. This 10-year revision schedule will be long enough to be practical in terms of administrative loads but short enough to be responsive to changing conditions, monitoring and research results, and adaptive management revisions.

div.head: 10-YEAR REVIEW PROCEDURE
div.p: In summary, the RIWAP evaluation, review and revision schedule will have the following benchmarks:

div.head: RIWAP REVIEW PROCESS
div.p: Within RIDEM, individual divisions prepare work plans, program narratives, or strategies every year.

The RIWAP priority conservation actions (including research, monitoring, inventory, and management actions) will be incorporated into the DFW annual work strategy, with the implementation of the RIWAP identified as its own objective. The RIDEM DFW's work strategy is formatted with each objective reporting on trends, problems and initiatives. This format lends itself to ready incorporation of the RIWAP, which also includes detailed information on trends (status and condition), problems (threats) and initiatives (conservation actions). Each objective in the RIDEM DFW Work Strategy is further delineated with environmental indicators, strategies, activities (conservation actions) and performance measure review schedules. RIDEM DMF prepares a strategic plan every five years, which incorporates the Division's setting of annual research priorities and proposed work plans. This annual exercise integrates RIWAP implementation and tracks progress.

Both the DFW and DMF have adopted the Wildlife TRACS system for reporting (as described in Chapter 5). As a result, RIDEM DFW and DMF have an existing administrative framework in which to incorporate the RIWAP review and revision. Highest priority conservation actions can subsequently be updated and included in each annual Work Strategy, allowing for adaptive management, performance review and institutionalization of RIWAP implementation.

div.head: CHAPTER 6
div.p: Partner & Public Participation

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: The RIWAP is a robust and dynamic plan and required multiple levels of input and review. Not only does RIDEM depend on and collaborate with partners for monitoring, research, and conservation (see Chapter 4 and RIWAP database), but RIDEM's goal for this SWAP was to increase the usefulness of plan content and design for the public so all Rhode Islanders can engage in meaningful stewardship. This chapter describes how RIDEM coordinated with partners and engaged the public in the development of this RIWAP and how it will continue to do so in the implementation of this wildlife conservation strategy (Element 7).

div.head: PARTNER PARTICIPATION
div.p: Partners were included in many Taxa Teams (Appendix I), where their expertise, research, and perspectives enhanced the initial technical updates to the plan, and in each major phase of the RIWAP process thereafter. The RIWAP Taxa Teams, as described in Chapter 1, consisted of RIDEM staff from DFW and DMF and external experts. These experts were invited to collaborate with RIDEM to make initial decisions about SGCN, habitats, threats, and actions and included TNC, RINHS, URI, the Audubon Society of Rhode Island, Rhode Island Wild Plant Society, and more. Each partner was informed of the RIWAP targets, process, and schedule and was asked to incorporate the RIWAP information into their appropriate programs and plans.

Following the creation of the draft RIWAP database, over 170 additional external partners and experts were invited to review the draft before it was shared with the public. Partners were identified based on the list of 2015 partners (updated with 2025 contacts) as well as additional individuals identified by the Core Team and Taxa Teams. Partners were given latitude to review the entire draft plan, specific habitats or taxa, or even specific species based on their interest and expertise. Of the 179 individuals invited, 33 agreed to review (Appendix II). The USFWS was a key partner at this step. Feedback was collected via survey, and all feedback was reviewed and addressed to the highest possible extent (Appendix III).

Coordination with the federally recognized Narragansett Indian Tribe (NIT) consisted of consistent communication to provide updates on the revision process and products and invite their participation and input at any time in the process. The NIT was invited to review and comment on the draft RIWAP database and participate in meetings throughout the two-year process and the RIWAP Liaison offered to gather separately from the existing meeting structure. Concurrently but separate from the RIWAP revision process, NIT representatives and RIDEM leadership meet quarterly to maintain communications and discuss topics of mutual interest or concern, and RIDEM provided updates on and an invitation to engage with the RIWAP revision during these meetings. The NIT was responsive to RIDEM through both these processes but did not opt to provide feedback on or meet specifically to discuss the RIWAP. RIDEM will continue to engage NIT in RIWAP coordination and implementation in the future.

Regional partners are an audience for the RIWAP, and it is important that neighboring states, multi-state conservation organizations and other users can easily understand and participate with all SWAPs applicable to their work. Accordingly, the RIWAP Liaison participated on the steering committees that advised development of the Northeast Lexicon and Synthesis projects as well as to disseminate information to a wider-audience and receive public input throughout the process. RIWAP materials, progress updates, surveys, and events were posted on the site throughout the revision period to maximize public awareness and participation.

div.head: SURVEYS
div.p: RIDEM implemented a series of surveys to better understand Rhode Islander's awareness of the RIWAP, how they engaged with the 2025 revision, and what informational materials or tools they wanted from the RIWAP. The first survey measured the public's awareness, asking questions like, were you aware of the RIWAP before taking this survey, how important is conservation to you, and what are the largest threats facing RI wildlife. This survey received 860 responses and showed that, while most Rhode Islanders (75%) were unaware of the RIWAP, 96% of respondents feel it is very important to conserve Rhode Island's fish and wildlife. This prompted the outreach team to focus on broader public participation and education about the RIWAP, resulting in community workshops to educate the public about the RIWAP before soliciting their feedback on the content of the plan.

The second survey intended to collect public feedback on the over RIWAP outreach process to understand if it was effective, what didn't work, and lessons for the future. Unfortunately, this survey only received 24 responses and therefore RIDEM was unable to draw meaningful conclusions. However, the discrepancy between interest in survey 1 and 2 might suggest that most folks who engage with the RIWAP do so indirectly, through the information and messaging it contains delivered through RIDEM staff and partners throughout the year in restoration updates, newsletters, outreach efforts, website content, family programs, newsletters, and social media. A final survey will be solicited following the RIWAP submission to USFWS to better understand desired and needed RIWAPrelated outreach (educational materials, public guides, printed materials, etc.).

div.head: WORKSHOPS
div.p: RIDEM hosted two community workshops (one in-person and one virtual) to provide an introduction to the RIWAP and prepare the public to review the draft plan. The workshops covered background on the SWG program, SWAP requirements, examples of SGCN and their habitats, threats, and actions, outreach products created by the 2015 RIWAP, and major changes between the 2015 and proposed 2025 RIWAP, including the web-enabled database. Following the presentation, there was a questionand-answer period; this took the form of an informal conversation in the in-person workshop, and viewers submitted questions to be answered live during the virtual one. The virtual workshop was recorded and posted on the RIDEM website for future access. Appendix IV includes questions asked during public workshops and how they were addressed. Individuals whose questions were not answered live but did not provide contact information did not receive any further contact.

div.head: PUBLIC REVIEW
div.p: Following partner review and updates to reflect the input received, an updated draft plan was shared with the public for input and feedback. The public was given 30 days to review the draft database plan and provide feedback. Similar to the partner feedback, public feedback was collected via survey and addressed to the highest extent possible, and the database was updated to reflect recommended changes where supported (Appendix IV).

div.head: FUTURE EFFORTS
div.p: These same efforts will be carried forward throughout the RIWAP's 10-year implementation period.

Increased public awareness will result in greater public involvement, buy-in, and participation, leading to improved coordination opportunities as well as new mechanisms to incorporate in future RIWAP revisions and/or implementation tools. Throughout the next decade, the RIWAP will be used to create educational and outreach materials to inform and engage the public. These materials will be used at events hosted by RIDEM, TNC, URI, RINHS, and other key partners. ORGANIZATION/AFFILIATION: N/A RESPONSE: In SWAPs, states are congressionally obligated to identify and focus on SGCN, yet to also address the "full array of wildlife" and wildlife-related issues in the process. This is a tall order for RI's more than 4,000 animal species alone, and the funding SWAPs secure is not up to the task. This is particularly true because conservation actions for diverse species with different needs can sometimes be at odds with one another. So, collective needs must be thoughtfully balanced in space and time on the landscape to support the full complement of native species. Considerable effort and expertise were expended to arrive at the proposed list of 542 SGCN and 83 SAPS plants and animals and to assign threats and actions at 4 priority tiers to these species and their habitats. Generally, species-specific actions contain finer detail than those that have been "rolled up" to higher levels. By virtue of the number of diverse species and habitats it must consider, it is necessarily far more broad and flexible in its prescriptions than, for example, a management plan for a single species, group of species, habitat, or property. Further, it was clarified that, while not often stated explicitly, there are very few actions in which RIDEM, or the state generally, is not at least an assumed partner in the action (e.g., for birds, "Work with state and local nonprofits and federal partners to conserve suitable habitat", if not the lead (e.g., statewide, "Continue partnership and coordination with RIDOT and local DPWs to integrate the RIWAP into the public infrastructure planning process"). Even for most actions appropriate at the level of an individual resident, such as eliminating herbicide and pesticide use in yards, minimizing outdoor light at night, and planting native plants, there is a charge to RIDEM and its partners to broaden education, outreach, and support to help residents understand and undertake these improvements.

As a first step, some major threat and action themes have been detailed in the RIWAP report now available as a complement to the full RIWAP database. For certain taxa, the RIWAP citations and additional resources can provide direction to more specific management plans that are incorporated by reference in the RIWAP, and the RIWAP Ecologist is on-hand during the RIWAP implementation cycle to work with partners and the public and to answer questions. Additionally, the RIWAP Conservation Opportunity Areas (COA) map, Community Guide, and 15 Small Things that Make a Big Difference for Wildlife, three key products that pulled out major themes and actions from the 2015 RIWAP for diverse audiences, remain relevant and available on the RIWAP page. ORGANIZATION/AFFILIATION: N/A RESPONSE: Respondent was contacted via email to provide more information. Since the release of the 2025 draft RIWAP database to the public, RIDEM has added a supplementary RIWAP narrative. This report covers the revision process elements that a database cannot, but it also highlights major themes, such as some important actions since 2015 that were achieved or are not yet begun. Still, shortcomings in tracking and monitoring are an important concern shared by RIDEM. SWAPs are supposed to identify all the conservation actions necessary to recover the full suite of species and identify monitoring and adaptive management strategies, but RIDEM is limited by funding and resources. Another concern, one which the RIWAP report addresses, is that the path to recovery is typically long and complicated, so early tracking measures are more focused on achieving actions proven or reasonably expected to get results over the long term than the actual recovery that may take decades or more. Finally, one thing that is clear and has remained a priority through three decades of SWAPs is that individual species conservation is not practical for most species and that we must apply landscape geometry and systems thinking to safeguard most species. That is, we know that most species are suffering from the shrinking and/or degradation of their habitat, with many specific examples of this detailed in the RIWAP database. This is why the RIWAP Conservation Opportunity Areas mapping remains one of the state's most important planning tools and why the 2025 RIWAP calls out the standing need for better, more current underlying data to keep this mapping as instructive as possible as to the best places to apply limited state and partner resources to land conservation and strategic stewardship. Estuarine habitats are primarily governed by the degree of daily tidal exchange and consequent water salinity and include tidal creeks, tidal flats, and salt marshes. Protected coves, bays, and lagoons of Rhode Island estuarine waters contain tidal flats, dynamic habitats that become fully exposed at low tide and are formed from the deposition of estuarine silts, clays and marine animal detritus. Tidal flats support a large population of wildlife and are significant staging areas for large concentrations of migrating sandpipers, terns, plovers, and other shorebirds and waterfowl.

Prudence Island in Narragansett BayHABITATSSubtidal estuarine aquatic eelgrass beds are also a valuable habitat in Rhode Island. Eelgrass plays a crucial role in the health of coastal systems because it provides critical habitat for juvenile marine life, helps stabilize sediments, and aids in filtering particles from the water column. The Narragansett Bay Estuary Program conducted survey of Narragansett Bay's approximately 96,000 acres in 1996 and found only 100 acres of Eelgrass remaining. The RI Eelgrass Mapping Taskforce began mapping all submerged aquatic vegetation (SAV) in all coastal RI waters in 2012. In 2021, SAV totaled 999 acres, 96% of which was eelgrass, while the remaining was widgeon grass or a mixture of eelgrass and widgeon grass, representing an approximately 28% decline in total SAV since 2012 (RI Eelgrass Mapping Taskforce, 2021). Most of those losses have been in the coastal ponds along the south shore and in the Narrow River, while Narragansett Bay has generally sustained the observed increase in SAV since the first comprehensive survey of SAV in 1996, including notable increases within the west passage of the Bay since 2012(Bradley et al. 2012).

note.p: New England portion of the Appalachian Forest, Rhode Island is naturally a forested place. There is general agreement among ecologists that prior to European settlement more than 90% of the state was forested by deciduous trees, primarily oaks and Red Maple. Coniferous forests constituted about 15% of the state's forest land with White Pine, Pitch Pine, and Hemlock the only naturally occurring upland species. Mature forests support a high diversity of wildlife species in an array of canopy, sub-canopy, shrub, and ground vegetation layers.

figure.figDesc: ). Rhode Island is the second most densely populated state, with more than 1.1 million residents (US Census 2024) occupying roughly 1,074 square miles. Transportation infrastructure that accompanies development compounds impacts by further fragmenting habitats and interrupting wildlife travel corridors to breeding, spawning, and wintering habitats. Coastal development and shoreline hardening exacerbate losses of beach and marsh habitats. Also typically accompanying development to varying degrees are changes to water quality and quantity, increased recreation pressure, and invasive species. Loss and fragmentation of natural lands, especially forests, are intimately linked to the effects of climate change because the dispersal and migration of forest plants and animals are disrupted by development and roads. Habitat loss is not only due to direct human disturbance; indirect changes like sea level rise or loss of seagrass due to changing environmental conditions are also having impacts on Rhode Island SGCN. For example, the loss of beach area due to sea level rise poses a threat to horseshoe crab spawning habitat.

Coordination with planning efforts is ongoing and includes updates to and execution of major, overarching guidance like Land Use 2025 State Land Use Policies and Plan (the State Guide Plan), which includes many other state plans as elements (e.g., Forest Action Plan, State Outdoor Recreation Plan) as well as local efforts that determine the execution of broad statewide guidance. Additionally, RIDEM has developed several conservation and management plans specifically to protect species and habitats throughout Rhode Island, but the absence of a strong regulatory framework for native species conservation beyond harvest limits, including for rare species, leaves fish and wildlife and the habitats that support them vulnerable.

note.p: During the 10-year period of 2015-2025 funding provided through the state's primary land conservation programs protected 7,000 acres with a land value of $90 million, and 53% of this value provided by federal and local contributions. When added to land already protected, more than 23% of the state has been preserved as open space, for recreation, and for agricultural use (RIDEM Division of Planning and Development 2026).

figure.figDesc: of the most concerning compounding effects of climate change and other threats is that, although climate pressures are causing species range shifts, development and roadways have created a matrix of inhospitable habitat that may inhibit such movement. Further, changes in marine species phenology are being observed in Rhode Island marine waters; for example, residency time of warm-water species is increasing. Additionally, increasing CO 2 concentrations have driven changes in pH, leading to ocean acidification. This restricts growth and reduces survivorship of shellfish, crustaceans, and other species with carbonate-based body structures.

note.p: Major advances in the development of climate-adaptation principles, strategies, and planning processes have occurred over the past few years, and there is a growing body of literature to draw from to develop state and local climate change adaptation strategies. An overriding recommendation is that in many cases the most efficient and effective approach will require a habitat or ecosystem-based perspective for conservation(AFWA 2009). Despite the mounting data on climate change, the Specific Actions and Concepts to Conserve Key Habitats detailed in Rubinoff et al. (2013) that helped guide climate change actions in the 2015 Plan remain mostly current and illustrative of the RIWAP's coarse-scale approach to addressing climate change threats to wildlife. Examples of these actions include protection and maintenance of managed and unmanaged forest blocks, conservation and management to maintain cool water temperatures in streams and ponds, and climate change advocacy and outreach.With over 500 SGCN, RI must focus on the most urgent needs and effective conservation actions. Species most vulnerable to climate change impacts include those with specialized habitat requirements, narrow environmental tolerances, dependence on specific environmental triggers or cues, or upon interspecies interactions, poor ability to disperse to or colonize a new, more suitable range, and long-lived species with few offspring and low/or low genetic variability(Staudinger, 2013).

Coordination with all federal, state, local, and tribal partners will be carried forward on a regular, multi-level basis throughout the RIWAP implementation and future revisions. RIDEM staff will inform and update partners and interested communities at partners' regularly scheduled meetings. SGCN and key habitat information will be presented, and these partners will be asked to incorporate them into their plans and programs as they are revised. In this manner, there will be an ongoing dialogue and information feedback loop in which partners' plans reflect the RIWAP targets and the RIWAP incorporates partners' revisions and updated plans and information.
